en: *The Brief Ritual for the Dharma Teachings of the Maṇiprabhā Buddha*, one fascicle.
Translated by the Venerable Buddhataṇḍa at the Xuanzhai Academy by imperial decree on the eighth day of the sixth month in the nineteenth year of the Kaiyuan era.

1. Regarding the Name and Teaching of the Buddha Entrusted with Transformation in This Land: First, the name of the Buddha in his original land is *Ise-de-u-lu-sin*, which is the Sanskrit term; translated, it means "Light-Messenger."
He is also titled the Dharma King Endowed with Wisdom,
and is likewise called the Buddha Maṇiprabha;
these are alternative names for my own Dharma-body manifested as the Supreme Physician of Great Wisdom and Radiance.
When he was about to transcend the world,
the two luminaries descended as spirits, dividing their light into three bodies.
Out of great compassion, he responded to and confronted the demonic armies.
Having personally received the pure instructions and commands of the Honored One of Radiance, he subsequently manifested his birth; thus he is called the "Messenger of Radiance.
Because his refined and true wisdom penetrates deeply and decisively resolves all doubts, he is called the "Dharma King Endowed with Wisdom."
Because his empty response accords with spiritual sageliness and his contemplation reaches ultimate perfection, he is titled Buddha Maṇiprabha.
Thus his radiance penetrates both the internal and external,
and his great wisdom reaches the very limits of the human and celestial realms.
It is for this reason that the Unsurpassed One’s rank is so lofty and honored;
it is for this reason that the King of Physicians dispenses the medicine of the Dharma.

Thus, the Lord Lao was entrusted with gestation by the Great Yang to flow forth its crystalline essence, while Śākyamuni received conception within the solar wheel to harmonize with its imagery. These three sages, drawing from the fundamental source of numinous spirit, are no different; their perfected natures persist eternally, all attaining the Way through a single thread of unity.
According to the long calendar of the Pārsīs, from the beginning of creation there were twelve *nakṣatras* (lunar mansions) governing the division of the years;
we have reached the eleventh *nakṣatra*, named Naḍuna, in its 227th year.
Śākyamuni appeared.
It was the twelfth period, known as the Era of the Succession of the Departure of Māra, the five hundred and twenty-seventh year.
The Buddha Maṇiprabha was born in the kingdom of Sulin, in the palace of King Badi, as the son of Queen Man-yen of the Kinsaka clan.
According to the *Pobī Changlì* (Calendar of Long Chronology), he was born on the eighth day of the second month in the thirteenth year of the Jian’an era of Emperor Xian of the Han dynasty;
thus, [the dates] correspond perfectly.
As for his being conceived through the endowment of a celestial mandate, it was as follows.
One who is pregnant while observing the fast and maintaining ritual purity is inherently pure;
she gives birth from her chest.
Standing out from the world and surpassing his peers,
he possesses nine divine verifications and five auspicious responses; such a person is born no ordinary being.
Furthermore, with the three vows, the four types of tranquility, the five truths, and the eight kinds of fearlessness—
his manifold virtues being perfectly complete—
they are beyond words. From the heavens down to humanity, one extols his virtues by speaking of how he uproots suffering and bestows happiness.
If it were not so, how could there be one born in a royal palace whose spirit is concentrated in the wisdom of the Way,
who clarifies the fundamental essence of the school, whose strategic intelligence is uniquely correct,
and whose physical constitution is solitary and eminent?
His measure encompasses heaven and earth;
his consciousness penetrates the sun and moon;
he opens up the great meaning of the two primal sources.
He reveals that their intrinsic natures are each distinct;
he expounds the profound texts concerning the three periods of time;
and he analyzes how causes and conditions are as disparate as tiles and shards.
He executed the wicked and protected the upright;
he stirred up the turbid and raised high the clear.
His expressions were concise.
Its principle is straightforward;
its practice is correct;
its realization is true.
Within sixty years, he revealed skillful means;
he invoked the Four Noble Beings as his majestic power and launched the Seven Sections as a vessel for crossing over.
The three halls were established to enshrine the Three Honored Ones;
following the Dharma of the Five Sciences, five tiers were arrayed.
This wondrous gateway is most exceptional.
Blessings extend to both the living and the deceased. The *Anoma-māyā-sūtra* states:
"One thousand three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa..."
The *kāṣāya* robe turned white and could not retain its dye.
The *Foshou sanmei hai jing* (Sutra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha) says:
When the Buddha Maṇiprabha appeared in the world,
he constantly bestowed light as his means of performing buddha-work.
The *Laozi huahu jing* states:
"I mounted the natural radiance of the Way’s vital energy (*daoqi*) and flew into the kingdom of King Sinara within the country of Sulin."
He manifested as a crown prince,
renounced his home to enter the Way,
and was named Maṇi who Turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
He expounded the teachings of the sūtras, precepts, concentration, wisdom,
and so forth, extending even to the three periods of time and the two schools.
From the luminous realms above down to the dark paths below,
all sentient beings pass through this after the mani-jewel.
"My age approaches fifty-nine;
my Dharma is destined to flourish.
Fifty-nine is forty-five.
For four hundred and fifty years,
his teachings were transmitted together with those of others in China;
until the fourth day of the first month in the second year of the Taishi era of the Jin dynasty, he finally ceased his transformative activity.
His body returned to true quiescence;
his teachings flowed to various lands,
transforming and guiding the common people.
From the Taishi era of the Jin dynasty until the present opening [of this record], nineteen years have passed, totaling four hundred and sixty years.
The records and evidence coincide;
the traces of the Sage are clearly manifest.
The teaching elucidates the fundamental principle to eliminate darkness and delusion;
the Dharma opens two natures, taking their differentiation as its gateway.
Thus, the commentary on the sūtra states:
If a person abandons conceptual discrimination,
they then extinguish all phenomena,
just like a practitioner who cultivates [the path].
"One should not dwell together with him.
It is further said:
"The crow returns to the void."
Beasts return to the forests and thickets;
righteousness returns to discernment;
the Way returns to nirvana.
If one does not examine the fundamental source,
to what can one turn for refuge?
This is the reality of the gate of practice.
The fruit and realization are the three palaces;
their nature is free from ignorance,
which is called the "single characteristic."
In this teaching, that which is called liberation is briefly cited here as a mere fraction of its full extent.
To manifest his progress in cultivation,
the Sanskrit original is quite complete;
it has not been recorded here in detail.
2. The Second Ritual of Form and Appearance. The Buddha Maṇiprabha possesses the supreme mark of a twelve-light-crowned, rounded crown;
his essence is fully endowed with great illumination and immeasurable secret meanings.
Her exquisite form was exceptionally transcendent,
peerless among humans and devas;
she was habitually dressed in plain white silk robes.
Emulating the four pure dharmakāyas,
he sits upon a white seat;
his image represents the union and separation of the five vajra grounds and the two realms.
The essential purport from beginning to end is clearly present within the true countenance;
by observing it, one may understand it.
The hundreds of thousands of sublime and wondrous spiritual manifestations are truly difficult to describe in their entirety. III.
Sūtra Diagrams and Ritual Implements (Jīngtúyí). This third section consists of seven works, including one diagram.

First, the *Da-i-Ōrinbu* (Great First Āvarta Section), translated as the *Scripture on the Wisdom that Thoroughly Exhausts the Source of All Phenomena*. Second, the *Jintei Kabu* (Section of the Seeking Gift), translated as the *Scripture on the Jewel Treasury of Pure Life*. Third, the *Daimanbu* (Niyāma Section), translated as the *Scripture on the Vinaya Treasury*, also known as the *Scripture on the Medicine Treasury*. Fourth, the *Arakanzabu* (Ārakṣaka Section), translated as the *Scripture on the Secret Dharma Treasury*. Fifth, the *Hakamatenyabu* (Bhagavatīya Section), translated as the *Scripture on the Realization of Past Teachings*. Sixth, the *Kokonbu* (Kaukunya Section), translated as the *Scripture on the Great Malla*. Seventh, the *Abufinbu* (Abhiyoga Section), translated as the *Scripture on Praise and Vows*. The *Da-mon Kawyōzu* (Great Gate Diagram of the Wings of the Load), translated as the *Diagram of the Two Great Sects*. The above are the seven great scriptures and their diagrams.
When the Buddha Maṇiprabha was about to descend and take his place,
the assembly of sages provided their support; he emerged to respond to those with whom he shared a karmic affinity.
On the day the Dharma was established,
he transmitted the five stages;
thereafter, for sixty years, he proclaimed the True Dharma.
The various disciples recorded these matters according to the events; they are not set forth here. IV. The Ritual of the Five Ranks 1.

**Musha** (translated as *Chengfajiaodaozhe*, "One Who Upholds the Dharma Teachings and the Path") 2. **Sabose** (translated as *Shifazhe*, "Attendant of the Dharma"), also titled *Fudotan* 3. **Mo-xi-si-de** (translated as *Fatangzhu*, "Master of the Dharma Hall"), numbering three hundred and sixty 4. **Aluohan** (translated as *Yiqiechunshanren*, "All Those of Pure Virtue") 5. **Nushayana** (translated as *Yiqiejingxintingzhe*, "All Those of Pure Faith and Listening") Those from A-luohan upwards all wear white caps and robes.
Only those of the *nōshaya* (novice) rank were permitted to continue wearing their former attire.
Thus, these five ranks received their respective instructions and all complied with the imperial decree.
To steadfastly maintain the prohibitions and precepts is called the path to liberation;
if one violates the precepts out of craving, it is not so.
One must not accept their instructions;
even if one is thoroughly versed in the seven sections of scripture and possesses outstanding eloquence,
if one commits a transgression, [the teaching cannot be received].
The five categories [of offenses] are not subsumed [within the four pārājikas], just as a tree’s flourishing depends entirely upon its roots;
if the roots are withered, the tree will surely dry up and perish.
Ārāḍa violated the precepts.
To look upon them as if they were dead is the rule for the community of monks to know and expel them according to the Dharma;
though the ocean is vast, it does not harbor a corpse.
If one conceals [one's transgressions], it is equivalent to breaking the precepts.

5. The Protocol for Monastic Quarters (Sīlaya-vidhi). Fifth Scripture on the Protocol for Monastic Quarters: 1. Hall for Diagrams and Scriptures 2. Hall for the Recitation of Precepts 3. Hall for Ritual Repentance 4. Hall for Instruction 5. Hall for Ailing Monks To the right, these five halls are established.
The community of practitioners shall dwell together and diligently cultivate wholesome deeds;
they must not establish private chambers, kitchens, or storehouses.
Every day he partook of a vegetarian meal,
remaining solemnly expectant for alms;
yet if there were no one to give, [he would simply continue].
Beggars shall be used to fill these roles;
however, they must be permitted to listen [to the teachings] but not allowed to keep slaves, domestic animals, or other such unlawful items.
For each monastery, three senior leaders shall be selected.
The first is Āvabhāsana, translated as "Praise and Vow Chief," who is specifically in charge of ritual affairs.
The second is Huluhuan, translated as "Instruction and Guidance Chief," who is specifically in charge of exhortation and encouragement.
The third is Upacārasena, translated as Yue-zhi (Moon-Direct);
he was exclusively in charge of offerings and almsgiving.
All must comply with these instructions;
one must not act according to one's own will. 6.
The Ritual for Leaving Home (Pravrajyā-vidhi), Part Six. First, the two schools are distinguished.
Those who seek to leave the household life must understand that the luminous and the dark each have their own principles,
and that their natures and dispositions are vastly different.
If one does not discern and identify [these], how can one practice?
Next, the three time periods are explained.
First, the prior limit; second, the middle limit; third, the posterior limit. Regarding the prior limit:
before heaven and earth existed, there was only the distinction between light and darkness.
The nature of clarity is wisdom;
the nature of darkness is delusion.
All movements and stillnesses [are thus].
There is nothing that does not oppose it.
As for the "intermediate limit":
once darkness has already encroached upon the light.
They indulge their passions in pursuit [of objects],
clearly entering from light into darkness,
as their physical forms shift and transform.
Greatly afflicted by weariness and seeking renunciation, they aspire to escape from this body, which is like a house on fire.
To labor the body in order to save one's nature is indeed the established principle of the holy teachings; yet,
to take that which is delusory as being true— this is an error.
Who would dare hear such a command?
This matter must be debated and resolved in order to seek the conditions for liberation.
The "future limit" refers to the completion of the work of transformation and teaching,
wherein both the true and the false return to their source.
When light returns to the great brightness,
darkness likewise returns to accumulated obscurity; thus,
the two principles each revert to their own state.
The two return to their source together.
Next, one contemplates the fourfold quiescent Dharma-body.
